title: Ogen: Anchoring Together Cultivating a Practice of Resilience

These masterpieces, found in UNESCO-listed sites such as San Vitale and the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, illuminate early Christian art. In this richly illustrated lecture, Columbia University art historian Sophia D’Addio explores their artistic innovations, symbolism, patrons, and enduring legacy. title: The Cuban Missile Crisis: Re-examining a Moment of Extreme Danger

The episode is often cited as a model of effective crisis management. However, historian Allen Pietrobon revisits the crisis to argue that it was less a triumph of leadership than a near-disaster averted largely by luck and fear.

title: Justice on Trial: The Dreyfus Affair and the Making of Modern France
desc: Historian and author Alexander Mikaberidze explores the Dreyfus Affair, the case that profoundly shaped modern French political culture. Beginning with the wrongful conviction of Jewish army officer Alfred Dreyfus in 1894, he traces how the controversy exposed divisions over justice, authority, nationalism, religion, and citizenship. Mikaberidze highlights the role of antisemitism, Émile Zola and the rise of intellectual activism, and the political struggles that reshaped the French Republic, leaving a legacy for civil rights, press freedom, democratic accountability, and the rule of law.

title: “Keep Calm and Carry On": England's Home Front in World War II

She also discusses how memories of World War II live on in British TV shows and films in the 21st century.

title: The Fairies of Winter: From Nisser to Huldufolk

Among the most compelling are the fairies of winter. Folklorists Sara Cleto and Brittany Warman explore winter fairies from different cultures, including some who love porridge and one who will suck your breath away if she catches you alone on a mountain during a snowstorm.

title: Palatine Chapel
desc: In the heart of Palermo, the Palatine Chapel represents a unique fusion of Norman, Byzantine, Islamic, and Latin artistic traditions. It was commissioned in the 12th century and reflects the multicultural character of Norman Sicily at its height. Italian Renaissance art expert Rocky Ruggiero highlights the chapel’s interior, where shimmering Byzantine mosaics depicting scenes from the Old and New Testaments cover the upper walls, set against richly carved wooden ceilings executed in the intricate muqarnas style of Islamic art. title: Slavery and the American Revolution
desc: Historian Richard Bell of the University of Maryland explores the American Revolution through the experiences of enslaved and free African Americans. With more than half a million African Americans living in slavery at the war’s outset, the conflict created new opportunities to pursue freedom. British promises of emancipation drew thousands away from rebel enslavers, making the Revolution a struggle over slavery as well as independence. While most remained enslaved after the war, more than 6,000 escaped on British ships, including over 3,000 Black loyalists evacuated from New York in 1783.

Author Daniel Stashower traces Dickens’ remarkable journey from childhood hardship to literary stardom, exploring both his triumphs and setbacks. Actor Scott Sedar brings Dickens’ enduring legacy to life with readings from some of his most celebrated works.

title: Mark Rothko’s Philosophy, Life, and Career
desc: Mark Rothko, a Russian-born American artist, felt like an outsider after immigrating to the U.S. at age 10. This sense of alienation shaped his Abstract Expressionist paintings, which he intended as spaces for viewers to confront deep human emotions and experience catharsis, much like Greek tragedies. Rothko grew frustrated that many people saw his richly colored works as decorative rather than engaging with their emotional and spiritual purpose. Join art historian Matthew Palczynski as he explores the life and work of this visionary artist. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: Nazis in South America: Notorious War Criminals Who Escaped Justice
desc: Writer and lecturer Adam Tanner examines how many Nazi war criminals escaped justice after World War II. Disguised as refugees and aided by sympathetic clergy, thousands obtained false identities and fled to Latin America. Among them were Adolf Eichmann, Franz Stangl, and Josef Mengele, all linked to major Holocaust atrocities. While some evaded capture for decades, determined Nazi hunters eventually tracked down and prosecuted a number of them, though many escaped justice permanently.

title: Venice's Artistic Revolution
desc: Around 1500, Venice reached the height of its wealth and cultural influence, surpassing Florence. Its lagoon setting, unique light, and access to Eastern pigments inspired a revolution in painting. At its center was Giovanni Bellini, whose brushwork and mastery of oil color shaped Giorgione and Titian. In a richly illustrated program, art historian Nigel McGilchrist traces Venice’s artistic rise and its gradual decline as influence shifted northward to the emerging powerhouses of Antwerp and Amsterdam. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: Preserving the Legacy of Women Astronomical "Computers"
desc: The Harvard Plate Stacks Astronomical Photographic Glass Plate Collection comprises over 500,000 glass plate negatives with astronomical annotations made by pioneering women who assisted the director of the Harvard Observatory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. These so-called astronomical computers made major discoveries and created vital reference catalogs. Thom Burns , curator of the collection, and advanced imaging pioneer Michael Toth discuss the collection’s history and how they use advanced technical imaging to preserve the work of these women.

title: The B-29 Superfortress: The Airplane That Changed World History
desc: The development of the B-29 Superfortress transformed World War II and reshaped the future of military aviation. Historian A.J. Baime explores the remarkable story of the aircraft that helped end the war and the leaders, engineers, and workers who made its creation possible. desc: Art historian Joseph Paul Cassar presents a chronological framework for studying Rembrandt's vast output, moving from his time as a young, ambitious prodigy in his hometown; his early success; the height of his societal and financial peak; years of hardship and more introspective work; and his poignant final years. title: What Mantises Reveal About Insect Evolution
desc: Praying mantises are some of the most captivating predators in the insect world, with their raptorial forelegs, uncanny stillness, and swiveling heads that seem almost alert to a human observer. But mantises are just one branch of a larger family tree called Dictyoptera , which also includes termites and cockroaches, giving scientists a unique window into how such different lifestyles could have arisen from shared ancestry. Entomologist Jessica Ware explores the evolutionary history of mantises, examining their hunting behavior, physiology, and relationships to their Dictyoptera relatives.

title: History for the Holidays: The Spirit of Celebrations Past
desc: The holiday season in America is a rich tapestry woven from diverse cultural threads, yet many of the customs cherished today are surprisingly recent inventions. Public historian Ken Turino traces how Christmas evolved from a rowdy, once-outlawed celebration into today’s family-centered holiday. He reveals how Christmas trees, holiday decorations, and even Santa Claus came to be, while highlighting traditions shaped by Spanish, French, Dutch, and other immigrant cultures.

title: The Persian Wars and the Birth of Classical Greece
desc: Historian Jeremy McInerney challenges the traditional view of the Persian Wars as a struggle between free Greeks and despotic Persians. He highlights the Persian Empire’s stability, tolerance, and cultural achievements, while noting that Athens often acted tyrannically toward fellow Greeks. Rather than an inevitable clash of civilizations, the wars emerged from political miscalculations, logistical problems, and mutual misunderstandings. The result is a more balanced and complex account of both sides.

title: The Stars of Harry Potter
desc: In the blockbuster book series Harry Potter , author J. K. Rowling gave wizard Sirius Black (Harry’s godfather) the name of the brightest star in the nighttime sky. And who can forget the nefarious Draco Malfoy, Harry’s Hogwarts nemesis? Fittingly, the constellation Draco is a serpent-like dragon that wraps around Polaris, the North Star. Follow Sky & Telescope ’s J. Kelly Beatty in a bit of whimsy as he explores the true nature of the celestial objects made famous by their literary namesakes.

Explore Jewish imposter syndrome, why the language of “bad Jews” can be so harmful, and why, despite that, so many of us find ourselves using it. title: Scandinavian Design
desc: Scandinavian design emerged in the early 20th century, promoting simplicity, craftsmanship, and functional beauty. Rooted in Nordic traditions, nature, and the concept of hygge (coziness), it emphasizes comfort and thoughtful living. Art historian Jennie Hirsh explores the cultural influences behind the movement and highlights innovators including Alvar Aalto, Arne Jacobsen, Hans Wegner, Finn Juhl, Verner Panton, and Poul Henningsen, whose groundbreaking work established Scandinavian design as a lasting global influence. title: The New United States in the Age of Sail
desc: After the American Revolution, U.S. merchants sought to resume global trade but lacked Royal Navy protection. Historian Carl Herzog of the USS Constitution Museum explains how Barbary corsairs threatened commerce by capturing ships and imprisoning sailors in the Mediterranean. Meanwhile, Americans debated the cost and consequences of funding a standing Navy. Despite controversy and limits, Congress approved its creation, helping secure safer trade routes and expand American commerce in the early 19th century.

title: Lucille Ball: The Fabulous First Lady of Funny
desc: Come for the laughs, from the chocolate factory and nightclub antics with Desi to a spoonful of “Vitameatavegamin,” and stay for the story of Lucille Ball, the groundbreaking comedian who transformed television. Defying executives, she insisted Desi Arnaz play her husband on-screen, shattered taboos, changed how Americans watched TV, and became the first woman to lead a major Hollywood studio. title: The Olmsted in All of Us: The Legacy of America's Greatest Landscape Architect
desc: From Central Park to the U.S. Capitol and White House grounds, Frederick Law Olmsted and two generations of successor firms helped shape the American landscape and define landscape architecture. Birnbaum , founder and CEO of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, follows the Olmsted practice from 1857 to 1979, highlighting the designers and ideas that transformed parks, campuses, and cities. Their innovations, including park systems and landscape as infrastructure, continue to influence design today.

title: Dylan Thomas, Poet and Broadcaster
desc: Dylan Thomas, who remains one of the most popular Modernist poets of the 20th century asked his readers to "Love the words". From his early life in Wales to his untimely death, he honed his craft through varied forms of writing, including work for the BBC. Poet Nerys Williams highlights Thomas’s early life in Wales, his adventures in London, and travels in the United States. Through a close reading of key poems, prose extracts, and excerpts from his radio features, she considers Thomas’s evolution as a writer as well as his legacy.

title: It's a Wonderful Legacy: Frank Capra's Life, Films, and America
desc: Frank Capra, the director behind It Happened One Night, Mr. Smith Goes to Washington , and It’s a Wonderful Life , created some of the most storied films in American cinema. Author Sam Wasson and journalist Eric Deggans examine Capra’s lasting influence on American culture, the complexities and contradictions of his life, and the appeal of the films that made him one of Hollywood’s most celebrated storytellers.

title: Haley Heynderickx
desc: One of contemporary folk’s most quietly captivating voices, Heynderickx returns to the road for a rare run of solo performances following the release of her new album, What of Our Nature.
